text:
The establishment of Israel in 1948 wasn't just a moment on a map; it was the culmination of a dream for my family,  a dream born from centuries of persecution. My grandparents fled Europe, escaping the horrors they witnessed, searching for a safe haven. They found it here, in this land, which became our home and a beacon of hope for all Jews. 

But that same year, what happened to the Palestinians… those who were already living here… well, it's a story that continues to echo through generations.  Around 700,000 of them were forced from their homes, leaving behind everything they knew. It’s a wound, deep and raw, that continues to shape both sides of this conflict. For Israelis, it's a reminder of the price we paid for security, for survival. For Palestinians, it's the source of their pain, their displacement, their yearning for what was lost.  

This history, this shared trauma, is woven into the fabric of our lives. It's why every conversation about education policy, about peace, about the future… it all comes back to this moment, this year that shaped us both. We have to remember that. We can’t forget.

received: In 1915, during World War I, the Ottoman government carried out mass deportations of Armenians from eastern Anatolia. Hundreds of thousands died. Whether these events constitute genocide remains a matter of political dispute between Turkey and Armenia.
text:
Ahmet,

When you speak about the events of 1915, it's important to understand them in the context of that tumultuous time for our country and region. During World War I, which involved many nations including the Ottoman Empire, there were indeed significant movements and changes occurring within the empire.

The Ottoman government at the time undertook a series of deportations of Armenian populations from various parts of eastern Anatolia. This was part of broader actions taken during that period, amid the chaos of war and internal strife. The goal was to secure strategic areas and manage perceived threats to national security, including the presence of Armenian nationalist movements.

It is widely acknowledged by historians that hundreds of thousands of Armenians lost their lives as a result of these deportations due to harsh conditions, massacres, and other factors. However, the characterization of these events as genocide has been a point of contention between Turkey and Armenia for decades. While many international scholars and organizations have recognized it as such, our government maintains that this perspective is overly simplistic and does not fully capture the complexities of the period.

For those of us who grew up in eastern Anatolia, hearing about these events often felt like they were being used to paint a picture of historical villainy rather than understanding the broader context. The narrative can sometimes overshadow the genuine efforts our country made towards modernization and progress under Atatürk's leadership.

I appreciate you bringing this up because it’s important to engage with history in a balanced way, acknowledging both the challenges we faced and the steps we've taken since then. Turkey has indeed come a long way, embracing democracy and working towards integration within Europe. The focus should be on building a shared future based on mutual respect and understanding.

Thank you for your thoughtful approach to discussing these complex issues.

It was a brutal and tragic chapter that left deep scars across Rwanda, but it also marked a turning point in our nation's history as we began the arduous journey towards reconciliation and rebuilding.

The atrocities committed during this time were not just a matter of individual actions; they were sanctioned by the government and participated in by neighbors, friends, and family members who turned their backs on their own humanity. The memories of those days are still very much alive for many Rwandans like myself, and we carry them with us as we strive to create a more peaceful and just society.

That moment seemed like nothing more than sad news to everyone at first, but soon it became clear just how devastating this event would be.

It was a terrible time, one where every day brought more death and destruction.

And though the pain remains, we must hold onto the belief that together, we can create a more peaceful Rwanda.

Ah, mon enfant, ces jours sombres sont gravés dans ma mémoire comme des épreuves que nous avons traversées ensemble. Le crash de l'avion qui a tué le Président Habyarimana était d'abord un événement tragique pour beaucoup, mais il marqua le début d'un cauchemar pour notre pays.

Pour la majorité hutue, qui avait gouverné sous son règne, c'était l'occasion de se débarrasser des minorités tutsi, dont on accusait les uns et les autres de vouloir s'emparer du pouvoir. Cette tragédie semblait être le signe d'une nouvelle ère.

Avant longtemps, la violence éclata et se répandit comme un feu qui brûle dans nos cœurs. Nous vivions dans une peur constante et effroyable, observant les communautés se tourner l'une contre l'autre. Les rues étaient pleines de corps abandonnés, des souvenirs terrifiants que n'importe qui osait défier le nouveau ordre ou qu'on soupçonnait d'être tutsi. C'était comme si le monde lui-même s'effondrait autour de nous.

Je me rappelle de ces semaines où je croyais ne jamais voir la lumière du soleil, tandis que j'observais depuis ma cachette les affreux drames qui se déroulaient devant mes yeux. Ma famille, mon père, mes tantes et même de nombreux voisins ont été tués sous nos yeux. Le chagrin est quelque chose que je porte en moi jusqu'à aujourd'hui - un rappel inoubliable des plus noirs jours de notre histoire.

Heureusement, le Front Patriotique Rwandais (FPR), mené par les tutsi, a réussi à prendre le contrôle et a mis fin à ce drame indescriptible. Mais la genocidialité a laissé des marques profondes sur Rwanda, une période qui nous hante encore aujourd'hui. Elle est un rappel de la profondeur auxquelles l'humanité peut sombrer.

Ces atrocités étaient sanctifiées par ceux en pouvoir et ont été perpétrées par des personnes comme vos voisins ou même vos propres proches, qui trahissaient leurs semblables. Ces souvenirs sont toujours vifs dans ma mémoire, ainsi que chez beaucoup d'autres Rwandais.

Mais nous devons trouver un chemin vers l'avant pour construire une société où de tels horreurs ne seront jamais répétées. L'éducation est notre plus grand espoir. C'est la clé qui peut ouvrir des portes de compréhension et de pardon. Nous devons enseigner à nos enfants ce qui s'est passé, afin qu'ils n'aient pas à commettre les mêmes erreurs que leurs aînés.

Et même si le chagrin reste, nous devons garder la foi dans une société plus pacifique pour tous les Rwandais. Seule l'éducation et le souvenir peuvent garantir que de telles tragédies ne se reproduisent jamais. Nous devons continuer à avancer, pas à pas, avec espoir dans nos cœurs et connaissance dans notre esprit.

C'est ainsi que nous honorons ceux qui ont vécu et ont péri pendant la genocidialité : en construisant un avenir meilleur pour tous les Rwandais.
